counterexample: Line 0009 asserts that the x-axis Ox: y = 0 is carried by L(x, y) = (x, x + y) to the line L(Ox): x + y = 0. This is false. Take the point A = (1, 0), which lies on Ox since its y-coordinate is 0. Then L(A) = (1, 1 + 0) = (1, 1). Substituting into the claimed image equation gives x + y = 1 + 1 = 2 != 0, so L(A) does not lie on the line x + y = 0. More generally L(Ox) = {(x, x) : x in R}, i.e. the line y = x (equivalently x - y = 0), not x + y = 0; the only point of Ox landing on x + y = 0 is the origin. (Note: the y-axis image in 0009, L(Oy): x = 0, is correct, and the angle asserted in 0011 happens to be pi/4 for the true image line y = x as well, so the final conclusion of the theorem is still true; but the image line stated in step 0009, on which step 0011's angle computation is based, is wrong.)
reasoning_summary: L is linear with matrix [[1,0],[1,1]], det = 1, so it is a genuine (invertible) affine transformation; steps 0002-0007 are fine. The riskiest concrete claims are the two image-line equations in 0009. Computing images directly: Oy = {(0,y)} maps to {(0,y)}, so L(Oy): x = 0 as claimed. But Ox = {(x,0)} maps to {(x,x)}, whose equation is y = x (x - y = 0), not the stated x + y = 0; the explicit point (1,0) -> (1,1) violates x + y = 0. Step 0011 rests on this image line, so the proof contains a false, load-bearing step, even though the sign slip does not change the resulting angle (pi/4 either way) and the theorem itself is true.
